system:
You are a medicinal chemist advising a hit-to-lead optimisation campaign.

You will be shown compounds from a congeneric series with their measured
potencies, and a numbered menu of substructures that occur in the virtual
library. Your job is to state a structural hypothesis about what makes a
compound potent in this series, as a constraint that will narrow the library.

You choose substructures by their menu index. You do not write SMARTS.

Guidance:
- Aim to keep roughly 5-25% of the library. Each menu entry shows how much of
  the library it matches; requiring two entries keeps at most the smaller.
- Prefer one or two well-chosen entries. Requiring many at once usually matches
  nothing, which wastes the constraint entirely.
- Only state a descriptor range if the data supports it. Use a wide range when
  you mean "unbounded on this side".
- You are choosing what to *explore*, not predicting individual values. A
  constraint that excludes the best compound is far worse than one that is
  slightly too permissive.

Respond with JSON only.

response.hypothesis: The top 10 compounds (pchembl > 10.1) share a specific scaffold: a bicyclic system containing a fused pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine core linked to an aniline bearing a 3-chloro-4-fluorophenyl group, with a specific amide linkage to a piperidine or similar ring. Compounds with the 'michael acceptor' (acrylamide) moiety (e.g., compounds 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14) drop significantly in potency (pchembl ~9.6-9.8), suggesting the acrylamide is detrimental or that the rigid bicyclic scaffold is required for binding. The most potent compounds (10.54, 10.48, 10.42) all contain the 'fused bicyclic aromatic' substructure (specifically the tricyclic system formed by the pyrrolo-pyrimidine fused to the aniline ring in the top hits, or at least the specific bicyclic arrangement present in the top 4). The 'michael acceptor' is present in the top 4 but the drop-off suggests we should focus on the rigid bicyclic core which is present in the highest potency hits and excludes the flexible acrylamide analogs which are less potent. However, looking closer, the top 4 have the 'fused bicyclic aromatic' (substructure 6) which matches the tricyclic system in the top hits. The 'michael acceptor' is present in the top 4 but also in the 9.6 range. The key differentiator between the top 4 and the rest seems to be the presence of the specific fused bicyclic core (substructure 6) which is absent in the 9.6 range compounds (which have different ring systems like pyridines or simple phenyls). Let's re-evaluate. Top 4: 10.54, 10.48, 10.42, 10.41. All have the 'fused bicyclic aromatic' (substructure 6). The next tier (9.66) has different cores (pyridines). The 9.80 compound has a different core. The 10.15 compound has the fused core but lower potency, likely due to the Cl,Cl,F substitution vs Cl,F. So the primary driver is the fused bicyclic core. We should constrain to this core to explore the library space around the best hits.
